analysis.one_liner: Ends fracking's exemption from the Safe Drinking Water Act and requires companies to disclose the chemicals they inject underground.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Senator Casey and 12 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate environment committee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would close a loophole written into the Safe Drinking Water Act in 2005 that exempts hydraulic fracturing from the rules that apply to other kinds of underground injection. It would let the EPA regulate fracking as underground injection, let states take over enforcement of just the fracking rules, and require drilling companies to disclose, before and after each job, the chemicals and sand they pump into the ground — with the list posted on a public website. It also requires companies to hand over trade-secret chemical identities to doctors, first responders, or regulators during a medical emergency.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near fracking operations and drink groundwater: they would learn which chemicals are being injected near them, and regulators could treat fracking wells under the same drinking-water rules as other injection wells. First responders and doctors would get chemical identities in emergencies without waiting for a company's paperwork.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near fracking sites and their doctors

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the exemption that keeps fracking outside the Safe Drinking Water Act's underground injection program, putting those wells under the same permitting framework as other injection wells [S2][S3].

Requires operators to disclose intended and actually-used chemicals and proppants — including chemical constituents and safety data sheets — to the state or EPA, with the information verified and posted on a single searchable public website [S2][S3].

Requires immediate disclosure of trade-secret chemical identities to the state, EPA, a first responder, or a health care practitioner during a medical emergency, regardless of any confidentiality agreement [S2][S3].
Lets a state take over enforcement of just the fracking rules without assuming responsibility for every other kind of injection well, limiting federal preemption concerns [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies doing the fracking, who would face federal drinking-water permitting for fracking wells and would have to report the composition of their fluid mixtures; companies would keep proprietary formulas out of public view, but regulators and (in emergencies) medical personnel could see them.

drawbacks.text: Fracking operators would face a new layer of federal permitting under the Safe Drinking Water Act, which industry argues duplicates state oversight and adds cost and delay to wells that are currently permitted under state programs [S2].

Chemical disclosure reaches trade-secret formulas: while the bill bars public release of a proprietary formula [S3], companies would have to open those formulas to state and federal regulators and, in emergencies, to doctors and first responders.

The bill regulates fracking but does not ban it, and it leaves the public-disclosure carve-out for proprietary formulas in place, so the strongest form of chemical transparency — full public formulas — is not achieved even under the bill as written [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people living near fracking operations, the gains are concrete: knowing what is being injected underground, and doctors getting chemical identities in an emergency. The costs fall on drilling companies, which would take on a federal permitting layer and chemical reporting. The main honest criticism of the bill is that it stops short of full public disclosure of trade-secret formulas; the main criticism against it is cost and possible duplication of state regulation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up; no hearing, no vote, and it expired when the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Casey introduced the FRAC Act on March 18, 2015, joined by 11 other Democratic senators as original cosponsors, for a total of 12 cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S3][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S5].
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, so the bill died in committee [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies kept the fracking exemption from the Safe Drinking Water Act and avoided any federal chemical-disclosure mandate; residents near fracking sites gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fracking operators, who kept their exemption

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey Jr.
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FRAC Act to repeal fracking's Safe Drinking Water Act exemption and require chemical disclosure.

for.name: 12 of 46 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; all 12 cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it for the rest of the 114th Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed the FRAC Act and federal regulation of fracking fluids in prior and current Congresses, arguing state regulation was sufficient.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced out of the Republican-led environment committee.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers using hydraulic fracturing
industries.note: The bill would strip fracking's exemption from the Safe Drinking Water Act and require chemical disclosure before and after each job. Operators would face a federal permitting layer and reporting duties; the benefit to nearby residents is knowing what is being injected under their land.

Suppliers would have to disclose chemical constituents and safety data sheets to regulators, and trade-secret identities would become available to doctors and first responders in emergencies. They would retain protection from public release of proprietary formulas, softening the blow.
